messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 44, Somchai had built a life that seemed orderly from the outside: he worked long shifts as a nurse, came home to his wife, and tried to keep up the steady routines that had always made him feel useful and in control. That order cracked on an evening walk after a late shift, when two men stepped out near the car park outside a corner shop, one of them blocking his path while the other yanked at his bag and shoved him hard against the wall. Somchai remembered the smell of exhaust, the harsh fluorescent light, and the shock of his shoulder and ribs striking the bricks; afterward, what stayed with him was not a full story but a sequence of vivid pictures, almost like photographs, each frame fixed and bright in his mind. He could see the angle of the men’s faces, the hand on his jacket, the pavement under his shoes, and when the memory came back it brought a sharp, bodily ache in the same places that had been bruised that night. From the beginning he was left with the sense that there was something about him that had made it happen, that nothing good could happen to him anymore, and that he had no future that felt secure.

Those beliefs settled quickly into the way Somchai moved through the world. He started arranging his day around what felt safest, choosing where to sit in restaurants, in staff rooms, and even on the bus based on which seat gave him the best view of the door or the most protection from being approached. At work on the ward he kept his mind occupied all the time so he would not drift back to the mugging, but the effort of constant distraction made him tired and irritable. He checked mirrors repeatedly, and as he left the hospital at night he scanned doorways, parked cars, and the edges of the car park, still expecting danger to be waiting just out of sight. Because he believed something in him had drawn the attack, he became more watchful in a way that made the world seem even less forgiving; every shadow confirmed the feeling that he was vulnerable and that his future had already narrowed.

The more he tried to protect himself, the more the event seemed to stay alive in his mind. His scanning of the ward corridors and parking areas, and his habit of looking behind him whenever he heard footsteps, kept the robbery in a constant state of near-presence, so that ordinary moments began to cue the same images of the wall, the hands, and the force of the shove. At night he slept badly, waking again and again, and each broken stretch of sleep left the pictures of the assault closer to the surface. In the mornings he would replay the night in fragments, and the more he searched for signs of threat, the more the memory returned in those sharp visual flashes, accompanied by the same physical pain in his shoulder and ribs. Somchai came to read these intrusions as proof that he was damaged and that his life had already been reduced to waiting for the next attack.

His self-blame deepened alongside those symptoms. Because he was constantly checking his surroundings and choosing protected seats, he felt confirmed in the belief that he was not the sort of man who could simply relax or trust that he would be safe; the very effort of staying safe seemed to tell him he had failed in some basic way. When the images returned at work, he would become more tense and vigilant, and afterward he would judge himself for being unable to put the event behind him. That judgement fed the thought that there was something intrinsic in him that had brought this on, and with it the conviction that nothing good could happen to him anymore. Even at home, his wife noticed that he sat with his back to the wall and glanced into mirrors as he passed, as if the world might catch him unprepared from behind.

By the time he sought help, Somchai was exhausted by the cycle of being on guard, sleeping poorly, and feeling that the mugging still defined what his life could become. He had not told many people how often he looked behind him, how carefully he chose seats, or how much effort it took to keep his mind busy during a shift, but these habits had narrowed his days and strained his sense of himself as a capable husband and nurse. What brought him in was the fear that he would never feel safe again, and the dawning dread that his children and wife were beginning to see him as permanently changed. He hoped, with some uncertainty, that treatment might help him stop living as though the attack were still happening, but he was most afraid that the future he had imagined had already been taken from him.
